verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. A psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a heading, but it tells the cast something. The poem was handed to a leader of public worship, so a cry that sounds private was meant for the congregation to sing and to own. The Hebrew verse numbering counts this line as verse 1, which is why the KJV's opening 'How long' is verse 2 in the Hebrew. The meaning of 'choirmaster' (lamnatzeach) is not certain: it comes from a root meaning to be pre-eminent or to oversee, and the Targum reads it as 'to praise'. The KJV's 'chief Musician' is a fair guess. The 'to David' (ledavid) can mean by, for, or about David; the tradition cited by Radak places it in David's time of trouble, or reads it as the voice of the exile.

philological_notes.note: A participle of the root 'to excel, to oversee', with the preposition 'to' or 'for'. It heads fifty-five psalms and probably names the overseer of the temple music. The exact liturgical duty is unknown.
The preposition lamed can mean 'of, by, for, concerning'. The heading alone does not settle authorship; Radak takes it as David's own prayer, or the exile speaking in his words.

verses.translation_literal: Until when, YHWH, will you forget me, unto the end? Until when will you hide your face from me?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, LORD? How long will you forget me? Is it for ever? How long will you hide your face from me?
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens on a question that has no answer yet, and it asks it twice. Play it as a man who has asked it so many times that the words wear thin. 'Until when' (ad-anah) is the sufferer's oldest phrase; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'how long'. The verb 'forget' does not mean absent-mindedness. In the Bible God 'remembers' when he acts (Gen 8:1, 30:22), so to be forgotten is to be left without help. 'Hide your face' is the ancient picture of a king who turns away and will not receive a petitioner; to see the king's face was to be granted an audience. The KJV's 'for ever?' makes a separate question of one Hebrew word, netzach, and the KJV splits the line where the Hebrew does not; the Hebrew runs 'will you forget me, unto the end'. Four times in the psalm the cry 'how long' returns (verses 2 and 3 in the Hebrew), and Rashi and Radak, citing the midrash, hear four exiles in it. That is a later reading, a rich one, but the scene itself is one person's pain.

philological_notes.note: 'Until where / until when'. A temporal question meaning 'how long'. The word anah is originally 'whither'. It appears twice here and twice in the next verse, a four-fold cry.

'You will forget me'. In biblical idiom God's forgetting is not a lapse of memory but the withholding of action; the opposite is 'to remember', meaning to act for someone. Radak reads it as leaving the speaker in enemy hands so that the nations say he is forgotten.
'Perpetuity, endurance, the end'. Meiri says that any very long time may be called netzach, as 'for ever' is said of a slave's service in Exodus 21:6, so the speaker is not claiming literal eternity.

verses.translation_literal: Until when will I set counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day? Until when will my enemy be exalted over me?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long must I turn my plans over and over in my own soul, with grief lodged in my heart, every day? How long will my enemy be lifted high above me?
verses.directors_commentary: The cry turns from God to the speaker's own inner life, and then outward to the enemy. Keep the voice low and tired. 'Set counsels in my soul' is a pointed phrase: the speaker is laying out plan after plan inside himself, because no one has answered him, and none of the plans works. The KJV's 'take counsel in my soul' and the ASV's are accurate but smooth it into something calm; the Hebrew has him setting down one plan after another with nothing to build. Metzudat David and Radak both read it as 'plans to escape'. 'Soul' (nefesh) is the whole breathing self, not a spiritual part. The Hebrew says 'sorrow by day' (yomam), and Radak and Meiri hear a deliberate contrast: even in the daytime, when a person is busy and forgets his grief, this man cannot. Night is when grief usually wakes; this man has it in the daylight too. 'Be exalted over me' (yarum alai) is the language of height: the enemy stands above him, as one who has climbed on a fallen man. The BBE's 'be in doubt' for the soul-line is not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'Set counsels': the verb is 'place, set', the noun 'advice, plan'. The speaker is the one giving himself advice, with no outside counsellor. Radak and Metzudat David read the counsels as plans for escape from trouble.
'By day'. Radak and Meiri read it as 'even in the daytime, when a busy person forgets his grief', or as 'every day'. Either way it stresses that the sorrow does not lift.
'Be lifted up, be exalted'. Used of the enemy it means to rise above and rule; Radak and Meiri say 'to have power over me'.

verses.translation_literal: Look! Answer me, YHWH my God! Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep the death.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at me. Answer me, LORD, my God. Give light back to my eyes, before I sleep and the sleep is death.
verses.directors_commentary: The questions stop and commands begin, three of them in a row, short and bare: look, answer, give light. This is a petitioner who has gone from asking 'how long' to demanding attention. The word 'answer' matters: the KJV's 'consider and hear me' turns a plain imperative to respond into a request to listen. Ibn Ezra reads 'look' as the answer to 'hide your face': the face is hidden, so he asks to be seen. The pair 'YHWH' and 'my God' is the covenant name and the personal claim together, and it is the first time the speaker calls God 'my' God. Until now the 'my' belonged to his own soul, his heart and his enemy; here he claims God as his. 'Give light to my eyes' has a concrete picture behind it. A dying or exhausted person's eyes dim; to have bright eyes is to be alive and strong (1 Sam 14:27, where Jonathan's eyes brighten after honey). So the request is for life and strength, not for religious insight, though Malbim and the Targum read it spiritually, and Metzudat David as a wise way out of the enemy's grip. The last phrase is stark in Hebrew: 'lest I sleep the death', with no 'of'. The KJV adds 'the sleep of'. Rashi cites Jeremiah 51:39, 'they will sleep a perpetual sleep', for death called sleep.

philological_notes.note: 'Look!', a hiphil imperative with a lengthening ending, the urgent form. Ibn Ezra sets it against 'hide your face' of verse 2: if he is looked at, the face is no longer hidden.

'Give light to my eyes.' Bright eyes mean life and vigour in Hebrew. Radak reads it as light in the darkness of exile; Metzudat David as wisdom to escape the enemy; Malbim as spiritual sight. The plain sense is revival.
'I sleep the death.' Death is the object of the verb, as Ibn Ezra notes: the noun stands in for the verb's force, 'sleep the sleep of death'. Rashi cites Jeremiah 51:39 for death named sleep.

verses.translation_literal: Lest my enemy say, 'I have prevailed over him,' my adversaries will exult when I am shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not let my enemy say, 'I have beaten him.' Do not let those who press me crow with joy when I stumble.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the speaker names what he fears most, and it is shame as much as death. In the honour-and-shame world of the ancient Near East, an enemy's boast, 'I have prevailed over him', was the public sign that a man's god had failed him. That is why the argument is aimed at God: Meiri reads the enemy's boast as a claim to have overcome God's own people's God. Notice the two words for the foe. The enemy (oyev) hates; the adversary (tzar) presses, the word comes from 'narrow', someone who squeezes you into a tight place. Malbim says the oyev wishes harm from afar while the tzar acts, and that both are watching. 'Am shaken' (emot) is the picture of feet slipping on a path; the KJV 'moved' is accurate but has lost the physical image. The ASV repeats 'lest' before the second clause, which the Hebrew does not; the sense is carried over by the same governing particle.

philological_notes.note: 'I have prevailed over him', a perfect with a pronoun suffix that makes the verb direct, though 'to be able' usually takes 'to'. Ibn Ezra explains the verb as intransitive with the suffix standing for 'to him'. The boast is a completed fact in the enemy's mouth.
'My adversaries' from the root 'to be narrow, to bind'. Malbim distinguishes the tzar, who actively squeezes, from the oyev, who only wishes ill.
'I am shaken, I totter', as of feet or a pillar giving way. Metzudat David reads it as 'when I tilt toward falling to the ground'.

verses.translation_literal: And I, in your covenant loyalty I have trusted; may my heart exult in your deliverance. I will sing to YHWH, for he has dealt fully with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, I have trusted in your steadfast love. Let my heart leap for joy at your rescue. I will sing to the LORD, for he has been good to me.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn comes with one small word, 'and I' (va'ani), set against the enemies of the last verse. Nothing in the situation has changed yet; the speaker has not been rescued. He has only decided where to stand. That is the director's key: do not play relief, play resolve. 'I have trusted' is a completed act, a trust already placed, and it rests on chesed, the loyalty owed inside a covenant, which the KJV's 'mercy' and the BBE's 'mercy' flatten into pity. Ibn Ezra puts it sharply: the speaker has no merit of his own to trust in, only God's covenant faithfulness. The verb 'rejoice' is in a wish form, 'may my heart exult', and then 'I will sing' is a resolution, a vow of praise to be paid. The last clause, 'he has dealt fully with me', is the surprise. The verb gamal means to deal with someone in full measure, and it is not clear whether it speaks of the past or of the certain future; the Hebrew text does not say what God dealt. Many readers take it as a perfect of certainty: so sure of rescue that he speaks of it as done. The BBE's 'given me my reward' pushes toward payment, which is not what the verb says here. The Hebrew counts this as one verse; the KJV splits it into two.

philological_notes.note: 'Your covenant loyalty'. Not pity but faithful commitment inside a bond. Ibn Ezra stresses that the speaker has no claim of his own and trusts only in this. Malbim says he trusts in chesed, not in reward he deserves.
'May it exult', a short, jussive-form verb. Malbim defines gil as joy at something good that was not expected.

'He has dealt fully with me.' The root means to deal out in full measure, for good or ill. The context makes it good. Metzudat David reads the tense as 'when he does deal kindly with me'; Malbim reads it as treating the speaker as worthy.
